title: Convexity and majorization descent
subtitle: G2 lecture 056000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Standalone slide treatment of the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix; authored derivations, worked calculations and local SVG diagrams.

slides.title: From list order to a norm inequality
slides.lead: Majorization is useful because convex symmetric measurements cannot increase when mass is redistributed more evenly.
body: Let F be a convex function on real coordinate lists, unchanged by permutations. A two-coordinate averaging step replaces a vector by a convex combination of it and a coordinate swap.
Convexity bounds F at the average by the corresponding average of its endpoint values. Symmetry makes both endpoint values equal, so the averaging step cannot increase F.
slides.takeaway: Convexity and symmetry make every coordinate-mixing step non-expansive.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 056000 · From list order to a norm inequality

slides.title: The two-coordinate transfer
slides.lead: Fix a pair of entries and interchange them with a swap π.
body: For 0≤t≤1, the vector (1−t)q+tπq preserves the pair’s sum. Choosing t=1/2 replaces both entries by their mean. Each mixed entry lies between the original two values.
For example (5,1) averages with (1,5) to give (3,3). This keeps total mass at six while decreasing the quadratic spread from 26 to 18.
slides.takeaway: A T-transform is a convex combination of a list and a two-coordinate swap.

slides.title: Why repeated transfers suffice
slides.lead: Suppose x is majorized by y and their totals agree.
body: A constructive finite-dimensional proof chooses the first coordinate where a current list differs from x, mixes it with a suitable later coordinate, and makes that entry agree while maintaining the relevant prefix bounds.
Each step can reduce the number of mismatched coordinates. After finitely many steps the current list reaches x; since F never increases along a step, F(x)≤F(y).
slides.takeaway: Finite transfer descent converts majorization into convex-function domination.

slides.title: Weak majorization needs one more operation
slides.lead: Averaging coordinates preserves total mass, but weak majorization permits a smaller total.
body: When x≺_w y, one can first reach an intermediate nonnegative list by permitted mixing and then shrink some coordinates to reach the smaller target list. The new operation must also be non-expansive for F.
Permutation symmetry alone does not control shrinking. An absolute or sign symmetry, combined with convexity, supplies the missing inequality.
slides.takeaway: Weak majorization adds coordinate shrinking to mass-preserving transfers.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 056000 · Weak majorization needs one more operation

slides.title: Sign symmetry proves coordinate-shrink monotonicity
slides.lead: Let q’ be obtained from q by changing one coordinate t·qⱼ for 0≤t≤1.
body: The shrunk list is a convex combination of q and the list with the jth sign flipped, with weights (1+t)/2 and (1−t)/2.
If F is convex and invariant under that sign flip, its value cannot increase. Applying this one coordinate at a time proves monotonicity on the nonnegative orthant.
slides.takeaway: Sign symmetry is exactly what makes coordinate shrinkage non-expansive.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 056000 · Sign symmetry proves coordinate-shrink monotonicity

slides.title: The weak-majorization comparison theorem
slides.lead: Combine T-transform descent with shrinking to cover all weakly majorized nonnegative lists.
body: For a convex function invariant under coordinate permutations and sign changes, any list x weakly majorized by y satisfies F(x)≤F(y). Symmetric gauges are norms with precisely these invariances.
The theorem is the reason that control of every Ky Fan sum automatically controls every unitarily invariant norm of a matrix.
slides.takeaway: Every symmetric gauge respects weak majorization.

slides.title: A numerical convexity check
slides.lead: Consider x=(3,3) and y=(5,1); the two lists have equal totals.
body: The Euclidean norms satisfy ||x||₂=√18 and ||y||₂=√26. The nuclear-style ℓ₁ sum equals six on both. The ℓ∞ values are three and five.
Different symmetric convex gauges measure different aspects of the spread, but all agree on the direction of the majorization comparison.
slides.takeaway: Convex symmetric norms can respond differently while preserving the same ordering.

slides.title: Convexity cannot be dropped
slides.lead: For exponent p below one, the expression (Σ|xᵢ|ᵖ)^{1/p} is not a norm.
body: Take p=1/2. For (3,3), the resulting quantity is (2√3)²=12. For (5,1), it is (√5+1)²≈10.47, reversing the desired comparison despite (3,3)≺(5,1).
The counterexample pinpoints why the convexity assumption in the gauge-dominance theorem is substantive.
slides.takeaway: A symmetric non-convex measurement may reverse majorization inequalities.

slides.title: Transfer the result to matrix norms
slides.lead: A unitarily invariant matrix norm is a symmetric gauge applied to the singular values.
body: If σ(A)≺_w σ(B), the gauge comparison gives ||A||Φ≤||B||Φ. We no longer need to prove the bound separately for Frobenius, nuclear, operator, and every Ky Fan norm.
This is the key bridge from singular-value prefix estimates to the family of norms in Davis–Kahan perturbation theorems.
slides.takeaway: One prefix-sum proof can dominate an entire invariant-norm family.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 056000 · Transfer the result to matrix norms

slides.title: Rebuild the descent argument
slides.lead: Prove the comparison by checking the two allowed elementary operations.
body: For a coordinate swap π, apply convexity to the mixture with πq. For a coordinate shrink, write it as a mixture with a sign-flipped vector. Each operation reduces or preserves the gauge.
A finite sequence of these operations realizes weak majorization and yields the general inequality. The constructive proof explains the assumptions and their separate roles.
slides.takeaway: Convexity, permutation symmetry, and sign symmetry each handle a precise step.
